title: Physiology of lactation and infant feeding
blurb: Explain how milk is made and released, why colostrum and responsive feeding matter, and what feeding choices mean for the health of women and babies.
question: On day 2, Aisha, 24, worries she has "no milk" because her baby wants to feed every hour and she can express only a few drops of thick yellow fluid. She asks whether to give formula. How should the midwife explain what is happening?

teach.body: Formally: lactation is the production and release of milk by the breasts after birth, driven by hormones and maintained by milk removal. In plain English: the more often and effectively milk is removed, the more milk is made. The first milk, colostrum, is small in volume but concentrated; around 2 to 4 days after birth the breasts become fuller as more mature milk comes in. The amount made rises or falls with how often the baby feeds.
teach.cite: NHS Breastfeeding: the first few days (reviewed Sept 2026); NMC SPM 3.14

teach.caption: Prolactin is higher at night, so night feeds help build supply. Early formula top-ups or dummies can lower supply.

rows.label: Triggered by
values: Suckling; baby's cry, sight or touch

rows.label: What she may notice
values: Tingling; baby's sucks slow to deep swallows

teach.caption: Stress and pain can slow the let-down, which is one reason calm, comfortable feeding positions matter.

items.label: Colostrum
items.sub: thick, golden, about a teaspoon per feed

items.label: At least 8-12 feeds in 24 h
items.sub: fewer but longer feeds over time

items: Early cues: getting restless, sucking fists or fingers, murmuring, turning the head and opening the mouth (rooting).
Feed during early cues: a crying baby is harder to attach.
Feed as often and for as long as the baby wants; a breastfed baby cannot be overfed (NG194 1.5.12).
Breastfeeding can also be offered for comfort, when her breasts feel full, or just for a cuddle.
Formula-fed babies CAN be overfed: pace bottle feeds and watch for signs of fullness (NG194 1.5.19).

Less diarrhoea and vomiting

Lower obesity risk

teach.caption: The woman's list shows conditions whose risk breastfeeding lowers. Any amount of breast milk helps, and benefits grow with duration.

teach.body: Discuss breastfeeding before and after birth: nutritional and health benefits for both, that it helps even if done for a short time, and how it soothes the baby (NG194 1.5.2). Involve the partner in supporting her (1.5.3). Acknowledge emotional, social, financial and environmental concerns and respect parents' choices (1.5.1). Breastfeeding women should take vitamin D (1.5.4; NG247: 10 micrograms daily), and she may breastfeed in any public space (Equality Act 2010).

The midwife explains that the thick yellow fluid is colostrum: concentrated, about a teaspoon per feed, which is all her baby needs now. Frequent feeds, even hourly, are normal and are what tell her body to make more milk; around days 2 to 4 her milk will come in. Formula top-ups now could reduce her supply. The midwife observes a feed to check attachment and swallowing, and explains night feeds help because prolactin is higher at night.
teach.cite: NHS Breastfeeding: the first few days; NICE NG194 1.5.12, 1.5.14

teach.text: "Feeding every hour means she has no milk" is a myth. Frequent feeding in the first days is normal and builds supply. The concern is a baby who is not feeding effectively (no rhythmic sucking or audible swallowing, few wet or dirty nappies), not one who feeds often.

items: Milk production works by supply and demand: frequent, effective removal builds supply.
Prolactin makes milk (higher at night); oxytocin releases it (let-down).
Colostrum: thick, golden, about a teaspoon per feed; milk comes in at about days 2 to 4.
Responsive feeding: feed on early cues; a breastfed baby cannot be overfed.
Breastfeeding lowers infection, SIDS and obesity risk for babies and several cancer and disease risks for women.

summary: You can now explain how milk is produced and released, why colostrum and frequent early feeds are normal, and how responsive feeding works. You can also describe the health effects of feeding choices for women and babies while respecting parents' decisions.

A.q: What is the main principle that controls how much breast milk a woman makes once breastfeeding is established?
options: How often and how well milk is removed
The size of her breasts before pregnancy
How much water she drinks each day
The time since her last meal
A.why: Milk supply works on supply and demand: each time the baby feeds, the body makes more milk for the next feed (NHS; NG194 1.5.12 lists the supply-and-demand nature of breastfeeding).

whyNot.1: Breast size does not determine milk supply; removal does.
whyNot.2: Drinking to thirst is sensible, but extra water does not drive production.
whyNot.3: Supply is driven by milk removal, not by her meal timing.

A.q: A student asks why night feeds matter in the early weeks. What is the best explanation?
options: Babies digest milk faster at night
Night milk contains no fat
Babies need less milk in the daytime
Prolactin levels are higher at night
A.why: NHS guidance: it is important to breastfeed at night because more prolactin is produced then, which builds up milk supply.

whyNot.0: Night feeds matter because of hormone levels, not faster digestion.
whyNot.2: Babies feed through day and night; night feeds matter because of prolactin.

A.q: Which description of colostrum is correct?
options: Thin, white and large in volume
Produced from day 5 after the birth
Thick, golden and about a teaspoon per feed
Clear fluid that should be expressed and discarded
A.why: NHS: colostrum is usually thick and golden yellow, very concentrated, and the baby needs only about a teaspoonful at each feed.

whyNot.0: Thin, white and plentiful describes more mature milk, which comes in later.
whyNot.1: Colostrum is produced from birth; mature milk comes in around days 2 to 4.
whyNot.3: Colostrum is valuable first food and should not be discarded.

B.q: Mother Ruth notices her baby's quick sucks change to slow, deep, rhythmic swallows a minute into the feed. What has happened?
options: The baby is falling asleep at the breast
The baby is poorly attached to the breast
Her milk supply has run out for this feed
The let-down reflex has released milk
B.why: NHS: when the milk lets down, the baby's quick sucks change to deep rhythmic swallows as the milk begins to flow.

whyNot.0: Deep rhythmic swallowing is active feeding, not falling asleep.
whyNot.1: Rhythmic sucking and audible swallowing are signs of effective feeding (NG194 1.5.14).
whyNot.2: Slower deep sucks show milk is flowing, not that it has run out.

B.q: Which is an early feeding cue the midwife should teach new parents to respond to?
options: Prolonged crying
Rooting with an open mouth
Arching away from the breast
Sleeping through a feed time
B.why: NHS: early hunger cues include getting restless, sucking fists or fingers, murmuring, and turning the head with an open mouth (rooting). Feeding during early cues is easier than when the baby is crying.

whyNot.0: Crying is a late cue; a crying baby is harder to feed.
whyNot.2: Arching away can be a sign of discomfort or fullness, not an early hunger cue.
whyNot.3: Sleeping through a feed is not a cue to feed.

B.q: Bella, 30, is formula feeding. Which statement about overfeeding is accurate according to NICE NG194?
options: Formula-fed babies can be overfed, so pace feeds
Formula-fed babies cannot be overfed if fed on demand
Overfeeding is a risk for breastfed babies too
Overfeeding is prevented by using larger teats
B.why: NG194 1.5.19: advise how to pace bottle feeding and recognise signs a baby has had enough, because it is possible to overfeed a formula-fed baby. NG194 1.5.12 notes a breastfed baby cannot be overfed.

whyNot.1: NICE states the opposite: formula-fed babies can be overfed.
whyNot.2: NG194 1.5.12 states it is not possible to overfeed a breastfed baby.
whyNot.3: Teat size is not the NICE strategy; paced, responsive bottle feeding is.

C.q: On day 3, Hope, 22, says her breasts suddenly feel full and warm, she is well, and her baby is feeding 10 times a day with plenty of wet nappies. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Early mastitis needing antibiotics
Her milk coming in, which is normal
Engorgement from overfeeding the baby
A sign she should stop night feeds
C.why: NHS: around 2 to 4 days after birth the breasts often become fuller as the milk comes in. She is well and her baby is feeding effectively, so this is expected.

whyNot.0: Mastitis is a red flag when redness and swelling persist over 24 hours despite self-care (NG194 1.2.4); a well woman with day-3 fullness has normal changes.
whyNot.2: A breastfed baby cannot be overfed (NG194 1.5.12).
whyNot.3: Night feeds help build supply because prolactin is higher at night.

C.q: Noor, 27, plans to give her baby a bottle of formula each evening from day 2 "so he sleeps". She wants to keep breastfeeding. What should the midwife explain?
options: Evening formula will increase her milk supply overall
Formula is needed because colostrum is too little
Early top-ups can lower supply; the choice is hers
She must stop breastfeeding if she uses formula
C.why: NHS: topping up with formula in the early weeks can lower milk supply. NG194 1.5.17 and 1.5.20: for women establishing breastfeeding who consider supplementing, explain the possible effects on breastfeeding and how to maintain supply, and support an informed decision.

whyNot.0: Formula reduces milk removal at the breast, which lowers supply.
whyNot.1: Colostrum is concentrated and normally enough; supplementing is sometimes, but not commonly, clinically indicated (NG194 1.5.12).
whyNot.3: Babies may be partially formula fed alongside breastfeeding (NG194 1.5.16).

C.q: Lina, 35, asks what breastfeeding might do for her own health. Which answer is supported by NHS information?
options: It lowers her risk of breast and ovarian cancer
It acts as reliable contraception from the birth
It raises her risk of osteoporosis in later life
It has no effect on her long-term health
C.why: NHS: breastfeeding lowers the mother's risk of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, obesity and diabetes.

whyNot.1: Breastfeeding is not reliable contraception from birth; the lactational amenorrhoea method has strict criteria.
whyNot.2: Breastfeeding lowers, not raises, her osteoporosis risk.
whyNot.3: Breastfeeding has several long-term health benefits for the woman.

reteach.title: A factory that runs on orders
reteach.question: Imagine the breast as a small factory. What tells it how much to make?

blocks.body: Every feed is an order. When the baby removes milk, prolactin tells the factory to make more; oxytocin is the conveyor belt that pushes milk out during the let-down. Fewer orders (formula top-ups, long gaps, dummies early on) mean the factory makes less. That is why frequent feeding in the first days is the solution, not the problem.

blocks.text: Do not mix up the hormones: PROLACTIN = PRODUCTION; OXYTOCIN = OUTFLOW (let-down).

explain.body: Prolactin drives milk production. It is higher at night, and frequent effective removal keeps production up. Early formula top-ups or dummies can lower supply.
explain.cite: NHS Breastfeeding: the first few days

items.label: feeds in 24 h in the first weeks

test.q: Which practice is most likely to lower a woman's milk supply in the early weeks?
options: Feeding through the night
Feeding on early cues
Skin-to-skin contact
Regular formula top-ups
test.why: NHS: in the early weeks, topping up with formula or giving a dummy can lower milk supply.

whyNot.0: Night feeds help because prolactin is higher at night.
whyNot.1: Responsive feeding on early cues supports supply.
whyNot.2: Skin-to-skin supports breastfeeding and helps babies attach.

explain.body: Suckling triggers the let-down reflex: muscles squeeze milk towards the nipple. She may feel tingling or nothing; the baby's sucks change to deep rhythmic swallows. Let-down can also happen when she hears her baby cry.
explain.cite: NHS Breastfeeding: the first few days

test.q: Which hormone is mainly responsible for the let-down reflex?
options: Oxytocin
Prolactin
Progesterone
Oestrogen
test.why: Oxytocin causes the muscle cells around the milk glands to contract, releasing milk (the let-down reflex).

whyNot.1: Prolactin drives milk production, not release.
whyNot.2: Falling progesterone after the placenta is delivered allows lactation to start; it does not trigger let-down.
whyNot.3: Oestrogen is not the let-down hormone.

explain.body: Colostrum is thick, golden and very concentrated; about a teaspoon per feed is enough. Babies may feed as often as hourly at first. Around days 2 to 4 the breasts feel fuller as more mature milk comes in.
explain.cite: NHS Breastfeeding: the first few days

test.q: On day 1, how much colostrum does a term baby typically take at each feed?
options: About 60 mL per feed
About 30 mL per feed
About a teaspoonful
About 150 mL per feed
test.why: NHS: colostrum is very concentrated, so the baby needs only a small amount, about a teaspoonful, at each feed.

whyNot.0: 60 mL is far more than a day-1 feed of colostrum.
whyNot.1: 30 mL is more than a typical day-1 colostrum feed.
whyNot.3: 150 mL is a large feed for an older baby, not a newborn on day 1.

explain.body: Breastfeeding reduces the baby's risk of infections, diarrhoea and vomiting, SIDS and obesity, and lowers the woman's risk of breast and ovarian cancer, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, obesity and diabetes. Exclusive breast milk is recommended for about the first 6 months. Respect parents' choices.
explain.cite: NHS Benefits of breastfeeding; NICE NG194 1.5.1

test.q: For about how long is exclusive breast milk recommended before solid foods are introduced?
options: About 6 weeks
About 3 months
About 6 months
About 12 months
test.why: NHS: giving nothing but breast milk is recommended for about the first 6 months (26 weeks), then breast milk alongside solid foods.

whyNot.0: 6 weeks is far shorter than the recommended period.
whyNot.1: 3 months is shorter than the 6-month recommendation.
whyNot.3: Solid foods are introduced from around 6 months, not 12.
